title: Extreme coastal El Niño reduces ocean carbon outgassing off Peru
content:
Abstract

The southeastern tropical Pacific exhibits strong El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO)-driven interannual carbon variability. Previous studies have established carbon response to basin-scale El Niño, but the response to coastal El Niño, a distinct mode confined to the Peruvian coast, remains poorly constrained. Using observation-based pCO2 products and a forced global physical-biogeochemical ocean model at ~ 0.5° horizontal resolution, we quantify and decompose the carbon response to the 2017 coastal El Niño. During this event, nearshore CO2 flux decreased by as much as 14.65 TgC yr−1, comparable to the extreme basin-scale events. This reduction was driven by weakened coastal winds that lowered gas transfer efficiency and suppressed upwelling of CO2-rich subsurface waters. Mean cross-shore circulation further transported low-pCO2 waters into the open ocean. This wind-driven and spatially confined coastal pathway is distinct from basin-scale El Niño, which suppresses outgassing through thermocline deepening, highlighting coastal El Niño as a distinct mode of carbon variability.
